ideas.title: Buy back time, not more things
ideas.idea:
Spending money to get time back may do more for your wellbeing than spending it on things.

Most of us feel short of time, yet reach for stuff when we have a spare few euro. In 2017 a team led by Ashley Whillans, with Elizabeth Dunn and colleagues, tested the alternative. They looked at what happens when people pay to shed a chore or a commute, such as a cleaner, a delivery, or an errand done by someone else. In a survey of more than 6,000 adults across four countries, those who spent money this way reported higher life satisfaction, and the link held at every income level. In a small field experiment, the same people felt happier after a time-saving purchase than after a material one.

The point is to notice that hours are scarcer than euro.
ideas.deep_dive:
The paper is "Buying time promotes happiness", published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2017 by Whillans, Dunn, Paul Smeets, Rene Bekkers and Michael Norton. It grew out of a plain observation: in rich countries, people report feeling more rushed than ever, and chronic time pressure is linked to lower wellbeing. Money is one of the few things that can be traded for time, yet most people do not do the trade.

The researchers combined two kinds of evidence. First, a survey of 6,271 adults in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands asked how much they spent each month on services that free up time, and how satisfied they were with life. People who spent more on time-saving purchases were more satisfied, and the pattern was similar for richer and poorer respondents. Only around 28 per cent reported spending anything this way, averaging about $148 a month.

Second, the team ran an experiment, because a survey cannot say which causes which. Sixty working adults in Canada were given $40 on two weekends, once to spend on a time-saving purchase and once on a material one. They rated their mood afterwards on a five-point scale. Time-saving purchases scored about 4.0 against about 3.7, and people felt less time stress.

The limits are real. The experiment was small and the sum modest. The survey shows a link, not proof. And the idea is about discretionary spending: it does nothing for those who cannot afford the basics, and the effect may differ across tasks and people.

examples.title: Four countries, one pattern
examples.text: Whillans and colleagues surveyed 6,271 working adults in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands. They asked about monthly spending on things that buy time, like paying someone to clean, cook or run errands. Those who did so reported greater life satisfaction, and the relationship held whether people earned a lot or a little. Only about 28 per cent reported any such spending, averaging roughly $148 a month. So the most common choice was to spend nothing on saving time at all, even among people who could afford it.

examples.title: The $40 weekend experiment
examples.text: To test cause and effect, the researchers recruited 60 working adults in Canada and gave each $40 on two separate weekends. On one, they had to spend it on a time-saving purchase, such as paying for a meal to be delivered or a task done for them. On the other, they bought a material item. Afterwards participants rated their happiness: about 4.0 out of 5 after the time-saving weekend, against about 3.7 after the material one. They also reported feeling less time pressure in the week they had bought time.

examples.title: What people say they would buy
examples.text: In a separate part of the study, 98 working adults were asked how they would spend an unexpected $40 windfall. Only 2 per cent of the purchases they described were time-saving ones. Most imagined spending it on goods or treats. Harvard Magazine's account of the work makes the same point from real life: people who outsource chores like housecleaning, or who live closer to work, tend to report being happier, yet the default for most of us is still to buy something we can hold.

visual.label: A simple strategy for happiness — Ashley Whillans, TEDxCambridge
visual.note: Listen for how she describes 'time poverty' and why people choose money over time even when it makes them feel worse.

why: Evidence: a survey of 6,271 adults in four countries plus a randomised experiment with 60 working adults in Canada, published in PNAS (2017).
Caveat: the experiment was small, the sum was only $40, and the survey shows a link rather than proof. It applies to people with spare money, not those struggling with basics.
ideas.try_this: What is one recurring chore you dislike that you could pay someone to do, or remove, for under €40 a month? Try it for four weeks and notice what you do with the time.

ideas.title: A rare coincidence isn't proof of guilt
ideas.idea:
"How unlikely is this by chance?" and "How likely is it that the accused is innocent?" are different questions, and mixing them up has put innocent people in prison.

This is the prosecutor's fallacy. Suppose an event is very rare if someone is innocent. It feels as though that makes innocence very unlikely too. It doesn't, because you have to compare it with the alternative explanation, which may be rarer still. Winning the lottery is a one-in-millions event, yet someone wins most weeks. A baby dying suddenly is rare; two such deaths in one family is rarer; but a mother murdering two of her own children is rarer again.

The habit worth building is simple: whenever you hear "the odds of this happening by chance are tiny", ask "compared with what?"
ideas.deep_dive:
The fallacy turns on a piece of probability that is easy to state and hard to feel. The chance of seeing this evidence if the person is innocent is not the same as the chance the person is innocent given this evidence. They only coincide if you ignore how rare the alternative is. The tool for getting it right is Bayes' theorem, which says you must weigh the likelihood of the evidence under each competing explanation, and also how plausible each explanation was to begin with.

Take the numbers from the most famous British case. Roy Meadow, a paediatrician, told Sally Clark's jury in 1999 that the chance of two cot deaths in an affluent, non-smoking family was about 1 in 73 million. He got there by taking a figure of roughly 1 in 8,500 for one such death and squaring it. That arithmetic assumes the deaths are independent, but cot death can run in families through shared genetic and environmental factors, so the true figure is higher. The Royal Statistical Society said there was no statistical basis for the number.

Then came the deeper mistake. Even if 1 in 73 million had been right, it describes how rare the deaths are. It does not say how likely it is that she was guilty. Double murder of babies is itself astronomically rare, and the jury needed to compare the two rarities, not hear only one.

The limit: this does not mean small probabilities are useless. It means they must always be set against the rival story. And in cases like these there is usually a prior question, whether any crime happened at all, that no probability can answer on its own.

examples.title: Sally Clark and the 73 million
examples.text: Sally Clark, a solicitor, lost two baby sons, in 1996 and 1998, and was convicted of murdering both in 1999. At trial, paediatrician Roy Meadow said the odds of two cot deaths in such a family were 1 in 73 million, a figure reached by squaring a single-death estimate of about 1 in 8,543. The Royal Statistical Society later criticised it. Her conviction was quashed by the Court of Appeal in January 2003 after it emerged that bacteriological evidence suggesting a natural death had not been disclosed. She had served more than three years and died in 2007.

examples.title: Lucia de Berk and 342 million
examples.text: Lucia de Berk, a Dutch nurse, was convicted in 2003 and 2004 of seven murders and three attempted murders, after deaths clustered on her shifts. A criminologist told the court the odds of this happening by chance were 1 in 342 million. The Royal Statistical Society later noted that, once real factors were allowed for, a cluster like it could be as likely as 1 in 25. The case was reopened in 2008 and she was cleared of all charges. The tiny number had done the work that evidence should have done.

images.caption: The Royal Courts of Justice on the Strand, London, home of the Court of Appeal that quashed Sally Clark's conviction in 2003.
images.credit: Anthony M / CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

visual.label: How juries are fooled by statistics — Peter Donnelly, TEDGlobal 2005
visual.note: Donnelly, an Oxford statistician, explains why people misjudge probabilities and walks through the Sally Clark case.

why: Evidence: the Clark and de Berk cases are documented in court records, the Criminal Cases Review Commission and Royal Statistical Society statements.
Caveat: these were extreme cases where a wrong number was presented to a jury as near-proof. In ordinary life the fix is just to ask what the competing explanation is and how likely it is.
ideas.try_this: Next time you read "the odds of this being a coincidence are a million to one", write down the rival explanation and ask honestly how likely that is.

ideas.title: Zebra stripes are a fly repellent
ideas.idea:
The most likely reason zebras have stripes is not camouflage or cooling, but to keep biting flies off.

For over a century, people offered tidy explanations: stripes dazzle lions, shed heat, help zebras recognise each other. In 2014 a team led by Tim Caro at the University of California, Davis, tested five of these ideas against data from across Africa. Only one lined up. Where biting flies such as horseflies and tsetse were worst, the animals' stripes were boldest and covered the most of their bodies. Later experiments backed this up. Horses dressed in zebra-striped coats attracted fewer landing flies than plain ones, and in Japan, cows painted with stripes drew roughly half as many bites as unpainted cows.

It is a good reminder that a satisfying story is not evidence, and that evolution often solves ordinary problems, such as being bitten.
ideas.deep_dive:
The puzzle is old, and the popular answers sounded plausible: stripes confuse predators, cool the body, or signal identity. What was missing was a direct, comparative test.

Caro and colleagues supplied one. They mapped the range and stripe pattern of the zebra species and their relatives, and set them against environmental variables, including temperature, habitat and the breeding conditions for tabanid flies (horseflies), tsetse and other biters. They found no consistent support for camouflage, predator avoidance, heat management or social interaction. The one factor that matched was the biting-fly hypothesis: stripe intensity was strongest where the flies were thickest.

Then came experiments on the how. When researchers watched horseflies approach captive zebras and domestic horses, the flies had trouble landing on the stripes. Dressing horses in striped coats had a similar effect. Biting flies also carry diseases such as trypanosomiasis, so avoiding bites is a real evolutionary advantage.

The limits matter. The cow trial used only six animals. A later study found sharply contrasting stripes deterred flies while faint ones did not, found no evidence that polarised light was the key, and a 2024 review notes how stripes work is still poorly understood. The fly explanation looks strong, but it is not the final word.

examples.title: A continent-wide comparison
examples.text: In 2014, Tim Caro's team at UC Davis published "The function of zebra stripes" in Nature Communications. They compared stripe patterns across zebras, horses and asses against five hypotheses: camouflage, predator avoidance, heat management, social function and fly avoidance. Stripes were most extensive where horseflies, tsetse and other biting flies were most troublesome, and there was no consistent support for any other explanation. Because the horsefly distribution wasn't mapped directly, they used the best breeding conditions for those flies as a stand-in.

examples.title: Painting cows in Japan
examples.text: In 2019, Tomoki Kojima and colleagues in Japan painted six Japanese Black cows in a Latin-square design: black-and-white stripes, black stripes only, or nothing. The black-and-white striped cows attracted significantly fewer biting flies than either of the others, roughly half as many in press coverage, and they showed fewer fly-repelling behaviours like head throws, ear beats and tail flicks. The authors saw it as a possible way to protect cattle without pesticides, though the trial was small and only a first step.

examples.title: Horses in zebra coats
examples.text: Caro and Martin How went further, watching horseflies as they tried to land on captive zebras and domestic horses, and testing horses dressed in zebra-striped coats. The flies repeatedly failed to land on the striped coats. A later study found that sharply contrasting stripes deterred flies while faintly contrasting ones did not. For a farmer or rider the practical lesson is real: bold contrast seems to disrupt a fly's landing, though exactly why is still being researched.

images.caption: Plains zebras in Maputo National Park, Mozambique. The bold stripes may matter less for predators than for the flies that bite them.
images.credit: Charlesjsharp / CC BY-SA, via Wikimedia Commons

why: Evidence: Caro et al. (Nature Communications, 2014) compared five hypotheses across species; field and cow experiments since then point the same way.
Caveat: the experimental samples are small, and how the stripes actually put flies off is still not understood. 'Biting flies' is the best-supported explanation, not a closed case.
ideas.try_this: Think of a 'just so' story you accept without evidence, about your work or your family. What would a direct test of it look like?

ideas.title: Everyone privately disagrees, and nobody says so
ideas.idea:
Groups can follow a norm that almost nobody privately believes in, because each person thinks everyone else does.

Psychologists call this pluralistic ignorance. Picture a lecture where the speaker asks if anyone is confused. Every hand stays down. Each student reads the stillness as proof that they alone are lost, so they keep quiet, and the silence confirms everyone else's reading. Nobody lies; everybody is misreading everybody. The effect is strongest where people judge others by behaviour (what they can see) while judging themselves by private feelings (what they can't).

In a classic study at Princeton, students were uneasy about the campus drinking culture but assumed the average student was comfortable with it. Left alone, that gap kept the culture going. A later study found that teaching students about this gap, in a peer-focused session, reduced their drinking.
ideas.deep_dive:
Much of the modern evidence comes from Deborah Prentice and Dale Miller at Princeton. In a 1993 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, they surveyed students about drinking on campus. Each rated their own comfort with campus drinking habits, and their estimate of the average student's comfort, on a scale of 0 to 10. The students consistently believed they were more uncomfortable than the typical student. That cannot be true of everyone at once.

What made the finding matter was what the misperception did. In their longitudinal study, a random sample of 25 male and 25 female sophomores was phoned in September and again in December. Over those months, the men shifted their own attitudes towards what they wrongly thought was the norm. Women did not change their attitudes, but felt more alienated. Perceived deviance, though illusory, tracked with campus alienation.

The remedy is information. Schroeder and Prentice tested this in 1998. Students were told about pluralistic ignorance, either in a group discussion focused on peers or in a session aimed at the individual. Four to six months later, those in the peer-oriented condition reported drinking significantly less.

The limits: the samples were small, the data were self-reports, and critics argue some of the effect is people genuinely updating from what they see, or simple measurement error. It also depends on a norm being publicly visible but privately doubted, which is not always the case.

examples.title: The Princeton drinking study
examples.text: In 1993, Prentice and Miller phoned a random sample of 50 Princeton sophomores, 25 women and 25 men, in September and again in December. Students rated their own comfort with campus drinking and that of the typical student on a 0 to 10 scale. They saw themselves as less comfortable than their peers, an impossible result if everyone was right. Over the term, male students' attitudes drifted towards the imagined norm, while female students kept their private views but felt more alienated from campus life. Believing you are the odd one out had real costs.

examples.title: Telling students the truth
examples.text: In 1998, Schroeder and Prentice tried to fix it. Students in a peer-oriented condition discussed pluralistic ignorance as a group problem. Four to six months later they reported drinking significantly less than students given an individually focused version. It is a rare case where a psychological bias was tackled directly, with a follow-up. The intervention was cheap: one session, aimed at getting private opinions into the open.

why: Evidence: Prentice & Miller (JPSP, 1993), 50 Princeton sophomores surveyed twice; Schroeder & Prentice (1998) tested an intervention with follow-up after 4 to 6 months.
Caveat: small samples and self-reported behaviour; some critics think part of the effect is real information-based conformity. It works best where a norm is visible but privately doubted.
ideas.try_this: Next time a room goes quiet after 'any objections?', say what you privately think, or ask the question you suspect others share, and see how many nod.

ideas.title: A volcano gave us Frankenstein and the bicycle
ideas.idea:
A single eruption on an Indonesian island in 1815 helped shape a famous novel and, plausibly, a vehicle you still ride.

When Mount Tambora blew in April 1815, it threw an estimated 100 cubic kilometres of debris into the sky, the biggest eruption in recorded history. Its sulphur veil dimmed the sun across the northern hemisphere, and 1816 became "the year without a summer": cold, wet, with failed harvests and soaring food prices. Locked indoors beside Lake Geneva, a group of writers, Lord Byron, Mary Shelley and John Polidori among them, passed the time with a ghost-story contest. It produced Frankenstein, The Vampyre and Byron's poem Darkness. The same shortage of oats is often said to have set a German inventor, Karl Drais, thinking about transport that needed no horse.

The lesson is how far distant events ripple: the connections are partly plausible rather than proven, but they are real enough to learn from.
ideas.deep_dive:
Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, began erupting in April 1815 and rated 7 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, the second-highest level. Its climactic blast around 10 April left a caldera about 6 km across and 1,100 m deep. Estimates of the human toll vary: roughly 10,000 deaths in the initial eruption, and up to 71,000 if the starvation and disease that followed are counted.

The global effect came from sulphur dioxide, which turns into tiny droplets high in the stratosphere and reflects sunlight. Average temperatures fell across the northern hemisphere in 1816. A 2019 study reported by CNN found that the cold summers of that year would not have happened without the eruption. In Europe and North America the result was crop failure, famine and food riots; the price of oats, which fed the horses that moved everything, rose sharply.

Historians are more cautious about the cultural links. The Villa Diodati gathering is well documented: on 16 June 1816, with bad weather keeping the party indoors, Byron proposed that each guest write a ghost story. Mary Shelley, then 18, began Frankenstein there. Polidori's The Vampyre and Byron's Darkness came out of the same summer. That the weather helped is clear; how much it mattered compared with the company and the reading of German horror stories is a judgement call.

The bicycle link is the shakiest. Drais is said to have been spurred by the lack of horse feed, and his first ride took place on 12 June 1817. Sources describe it as plausible and widely repeated, not settled.

examples.title: A summer that never came
examples.text: After Tambora, the northern hemisphere suffered a summer so cold that 1816 is remembered as the year without one. A 2019 study reported by CNN found that those cold summer temperatures wouldn't have been possible without the eruption. The cold and wet brought crop failures and famine across Europe and North America, and food prices soared. It was a climate shock with a single, identifiable cause on the other side of the world.

examples.title: Ghost stories at Lake Geneva
examples.text: In June 1816 Lord Byron rented the Villa Diodati near Geneva and hosted Percy and Mary Shelley, Claire Clairmont and John Polidori. Poor weather kept them indoors for days, and on 16 June Byron proposed that each write the scariest ghost story they could. Mary Shelley, then 18, began Frankenstein; Polidori wrote The Vampyre; Byron wrote the apocalyptic poem Darkness. Most accounts agree the gloomy weather shaped the mood, though how much is debated.

examples.title: Karl Drais and the running machine
examples.text: In 1817, the German inventor Karl Drais made the first recorded ride of his Laufmaschine, a wooden two-wheeler pushed along with the feet, from Mannheim towards Schwetzingen on 12 June. CNN and other accounts say that high oat prices after the cold harvest of 1816 helped inspire his search for transport that didn't depend on horses. The link is plausible rather than proven, and the machine itself did not catch on during his lifetime on the poor roads of the day.

images.caption: Map of the April 1815 Tambora eruption on Sumbawa, showing the explosion path and ashfall around the caldera.
images.credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor / CC BY-SA 3.0 (base map from NASA), via Wikimedia Commons

why: Evidence: the Tambora eruption and the cold of 1816 are well documented; a 2019 study found the cool summers would not have occurred without it.
Caveat: the Frankenstein link is plausible and widely cited, and the bicycle link is the weakest, so treat them as likely contributing factors rather than sole causes.
ideas.try_this: Pick one thing in your life that seems purely local, and trace a distant event, such as a harvest or a price rise, that may have shaped it.
